summary: Explains why congestion control is needed in the Internet and discusses what makes congestion control correct. It is a Best Current Practice document that guides designers of protocols and applications.

eli5.summary: If everyone drives onto a highway at full speed, it jams. This explains why traffic must slow down politely and what polite looks like.

questions: why do udp flows need congestion control
subtitle: Why the Internet needs every sender to back off when the network is overloaded, and what counts as doing it correctly.

tldr.problem: The Internet can suffer congestion collapse, where more load means less useful work, and a growing amount of traffic does not use TCP's congestion avoidance at all.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the dangers of congestion collapse and unfairness, defines TCP-compatible flows as the yardstick, and says which parts of a transport protocol the IETF should standardize.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice that states principles rather than a protocol. It has been updated by RFC 7141.

facts.label: Browser connection limit (RFC 2616)
facts.value: No more than 2 per server for a single-user client

today: RFC 2914 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 41) and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 7141. It states principles rather than a protocol, and it refers to TCP congestion control as then specified in RFC 2581.

sections.title: Why Congestion Control Matters
sections.content:
RFC 2914 is a general discussion of the principles of congestion control. It draws heavily on earlier RFCs, including RFC 2309 and RFC 2357, and on a paper by Floyd and Fall on end-to-end congestion control.

The RFC says that one of the keys to the success of the Internet has been the congestion avoidance mechanisms of TCP. TCP is still the dominant transport protocol, but an increasing number of applications choose not to use it. Examples are multicast traffic, streaming multimedia that does not need reliability, and short transfers such as DNS or routing messages. Much of this traffic uses neither bandwidth reservations nor end-to-end congestion control. The RFC states that continued use of end-to-end congestion control by best-effort traffic is critical for the stability of the Internet.

Differentiated and integrated services are out of scope. Some of their categories include a network guarantee of end-to-end bandwidth and so do not need end-to-end congestion control.
sections.eli5: Most computers slow down politely when the network gets crowded. More and more programs do not, so this RFC explains why everyone needs to keep slowing down to keep the Internet working.

sections.title: From Meltdown to Congestion Avoidance
sections.content:
The Internet's connectionless design is flexible and robust, but it needs careful design to give good service under heavy load. Neglecting the dynamics of packet forwarding can cause severe service degradation, or "Internet meltdown", technically called congestion collapse. It was first observed in the mid 1980s, as described in RFC 896.

The original TCP specification, RFC 793, had window-based flow control so a receiver could govern how much a sender sent. It noted that segments could be lost to errors or congestion, but it did not adjust the window dynamically in response to congestion. The original fix came from Van Jacobson, who from 1986 developed the congestion avoidance mechanisms now required in TCP implementations. TCP flows are called responsive because they back off when the network signals congestion by dropping packets.

The RFC adds that these mechanisms, while necessary and powerful, are not sufficient in all circumstances. A major open issue is the potential for future collapse from flows that do not use responsible end-to-end congestion control. RFC 896 had suggested in 1984 that gateways should detect and squelch misbehaving hosts, and current papers still propose that routers detect and penalize such flows.
sections.eli5: Long ago the Internet jammed up like a road after an accident, because computers kept resending data that was already on its way. A clever fix taught computers to back off when the road gets busy.

sections.title: Fairness and TCP-Compatible Flows
sections.content:
Besides collapse, the RFC worries about fairness for best-effort traffic. Because TCP backs off during congestion, many TCP connections can share a congested link reasonably equitably, but that depends on all flows running compatible congestion control algorithms.

The RFC warns of a spiral. Some TCP implementations may be buggy, and others may be deliberately more aggressive so a vendor can claim a "faster TCP". The logical end is effectively no congestion avoidance and a chronically congested Internet. Opening multiple connections to the same place, as some Web browsers have done, gets the same effect without changing the transport protocol. This raises the question of the right granularity of a flow. Quoting RFC 2309, natural answers are a single connection, a source and destination host pair, or a given source or destination host.

A flow is TCP-compatible if it behaves under congestion like a flow from a conformant TCP: it is responsive to congestion notification and, in steady state, uses no more bandwidth than a conformant TCP under comparable conditions (drop rate, RTT, MTU, and so on). The RFC sorts flows into three classes: TCP-compatible, unresponsive (they do not slow down when congestion occurs), and responsive but not TCP-compatible. The last two pose significant threats to Internet performance. The fairness of the initial slow-start also matters, especially for short-lived flows.

A third reason to use congestion control is a flow's own performance. With low statistical multiplexing or per-flow scheduling, the delay and loss a flow sees depend partly on its own sending rate.
sections.eli5: Sharing a pizza only works if everyone takes a fair slice. A flow that follows the same polite rules as TCP is fair, and one that grabs more than its share leaves others hungry.

sections.title: Congestion Collapse From Undelivered Packets
sections.content:
Informally, congestion collapse is when an increase in network load causes a decrease in the useful work done. The 1980s form, classical congestion collapse, came from TCP unnecessarily retransmitting packets that were in transit or already received. The RFC says modern TCP timer improvements and congestion control have largely corrected it.

A second form comes from undelivered packets: bandwidth is wasted on packets that are later dropped before they reach their destination. The RFC calls this probably the largest unresolved danger, driven by open-loop applications that do not use end-to-end congestion control. Even worse would be applications that increase their sending rate when drops increase, for example by adding more forward error correction.

Table 1 in the RFC shows a simulation of three TCP flows and one UDP flow over a congested 1.5 Mbps link. The UDP receiver sits behind a 128 Kbps access link, so most UDP packets above that rate are dropped at the last hop. As the UDP source rate rises, TCP goodput falls roughly linearly and UDP goodput stays nearly constant, so total goodput drops to a small fraction of the link.

The RFC names two ways to remove the danger. One is effective end-to-end congestion control by the end nodes, reducing the sending rate in the presence of loss. The other is a network guarantee that packets accepted at a congested link will reach the receiver. The two can be mixed for different traffic. Per-flow scheduling gives fairness but cannot be relied on to prevent collapse.
sections.eli5: Imagine a conveyor belt where a worker keeps loading boxes that fall off at the far end. The belt is busy, but nothing useful arrives, and other people's boxes get squeezed out.

sections.title: Forms of End-to-End Congestion Control
sections.content:
The RFC stresses that these concerns do not force every flow to use TCP's Additive-Increase Multiplicative-Decrease (AIMD) rule of halving the rate on each packet drop. Avoiding collapse from undelivered packets only needs a flow to avoid a high sending rate during a high, persistent drop rate. Collapse of this kind cannot happen where each flow crosses only one congested link or few packets are dropped downstream of the first one.

Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) lets routers set a bit instead of dropping packets, but it would not by itself remove the danger. Marking would replace dropping only at moderate congestion. When router buffers overflow, the router must still drop arriving packets.

Fairness with TCP is a significant but not crippling constraint. It could be relaxed with per-flow scheduling at all congested links, a diff-serv class scheduled apart from best-effort traffic, or a pricing-controlled environment. In today's FIFO-queue best-effort environment, a lack of fairness could let one flow starve out another. TCP-compatible procedures include rate-based variants of AIMD, AIMD with different parameters giving the same steady-state behavior, equation-based control that reacts to the long-term drop rate, and layered multicast where receivers join and leave groups.
sections.eli5: There is more than one way to be polite on the road. You can ease off the gas, brake gently or merge early, as long as you do not hog the lane.

sections.title: What the IETF Should Standardize
sections.content:
The RFC says standardizing a transport protocol covers what affects interoperability (information exchanged by the end nodes) and mechanisms deemed critical to performance, such as TCP cutting its congestion window after a packet drop. Implementation details that affect neither need no standard. One example is the details of Fast Recovery after a Fast Retransmit.

For new protocols, the process also aims to avoid a congestion control "arms race". RFC 2357 asks of reliable multicast proposals: is there a congestion control mechanism, how well does it perform, and when does it fail? It adds that mechanisms more aggressive than TCP face a great burden of proof. The RFC expects the same concerns to apply to unreliable and reliable unicast and unreliable multicast. On applications, RFC 2616 says a single-user client SHOULD NOT keep more than 2 connections with any server or proxy. The RFC also mentions the work on a Congestion Manager, which would let multiple connections to the same destination share congestion state.

A section on TCP-specific issues applies this test to each mechanism:

  • Slow-start: the sender starts with a small congestion window and at most doubles its rate per round trip. A larger initial window is a global matter; rate-based pacing and ending slow-start early are not.
  • AIMD: grow by at most one packet per round trip, halve on a congestion indication. Congestion control for pure ACKs would be a global matter.
  • Retransmit timers: on expiry, set ssthresh to half the window, slow-start, and double the timeout if the retransmission is itself unanswered. A timer scheme causing many premature expiries would matter.
  • Fast Retransmit: three duplicate acknowledgements infer a loss. Inferring loss after only one or two would matter; sending new data on a duplicate ACK would not.
sections.eli5: Rules are needed for things that affect everyone on the road, like speed limits. Small choices that only affect your own car, like which radio station to play, do not need a rule.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the whole document is about the risks of congestion control, or of having none. Because it proposes no specific mechanism, it presents no specific security measures, but it notes that such considerations should be weighed in IETF documents.

Individual mechanisms should be as robust as possible against end-nodes trying to subvert end-to-end congestion control. This is a particular concern for multicast, where traffic is widely distributed and individual receivers have more chances to fail to report congestion. The RFC also points to RFC 2309 on unresponsive flows and says research, engineering, measurement and deployment are still needed.

Since the Internet aggregates very large numbers of flows, subverting a few of them is a limited risk. The real risk is widespread deployment of many end-nodes that subvert congestion control.
sections.eli5: One person cutting in line does little harm. The trouble starts when lots of people do it, because then the line stops working.

items.title: Classical
items.text: Caused by TCP needlessly retransmitting packets already in transit or received. Largely fixed by modern TCP.

items.title: Undelivered packets
items.text: Bandwidth is spent on packets dropped before reaching the destination. Probably the largest unresolved danger.
